references.locator: Musculoskeletal trauma - compartment syndrome: clinical signs and initial management

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pain and Analgesia
references.locator: Acute pain after trauma - escalating analgesic requirement as a warning sign

tutor_context: Key facts: the tibia is the commonest site; the classic early features are pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and paraesthesia; the 'P' signs of pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late; compartment pressure measurement can help but should not delay surgical review; treatment is fasciotomy. Common misconceptions: that a palpable pulse or normal capillary refill excludes the diagnosis; that increasing opioids is the right response to escalating pain in a casted limb. Out of scope: pressure thresholds for fasciotomy.
plan: Tests recall of the earliest reliable sign of compartment syndrome in a casted tibial fracture (outcomes 1.4, 1.9). A woman has escalating pain despite opioids with preserved pulses and perfusion. Distractors are the late 'P' signs that interns commonly and dangerously wait for. Supported by the EMST manual.

stem: You are the intern at a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with a visiting surgeon and physician and specialist advice by phone. A 71-year-old woman who lives independently fell in her kitchen this morning and presents at 10:00 with left hip pain and inability to bear weight. X-ray confirms a displaced intracapsular fracture of the left neck of femur. She has well-controlled hypertension and takes no anticoagulants. Her pain has been assessed and treated, including a fascia iliaca block. The visiting surgeon is not due for 5 days and does not operate on hip fractures at this site. The nurse coordinator asks how urgently transfer to Adelaide must be arranged, because the next routine patient transport slot is in 3 days.
lead_in: According to the Australian Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard, within what time from presentation should she have surgery?

options.text: Within 24 hours
Within 36 hours
Within 48 hours
Within 72 hours

explanations.A: Twenty-four hours is not the national benchmark; it would be unachievable for many rural patients and is not what the Standard specifies.
explanations.B: The 2023 revision of the Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard states that a patient with a hip fracture should receive surgery within 36 hours of presentation, where there is no clinical contraindication, because earlier surgery reduces pain, delirium, complications and mortality. Presenting at 10:00 at a site that cannot operate, she must be transferred today, and the time of her first presentation to this hospital is the clock start, so the intern should ask the surgeon or orthogeriatric service in Adelaide to accept her now and request urgent rather than routine transport.
explanations.C: Forty-eight hours was the timeframe in the 2016 edition of the Standard and is still widely quoted as a benchmark, but the Standard was tightened in its 2023 revision.
explanations.D: Seventy-two hours exceeds the Standard and would mean waiting for the routine transport slot, which is exactly what the Standard is designed to prevent.

learning_point: The Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard expects surgery within 36 hours of first presentation, and the clock starts at the referring hospital, so a rural intern must arrange same-day transfer rather than wait for routine transport.
setting_note: In a rural hospital the time to surgery includes the transfer time, so the referral to the receiving orthopaedic service and the request for urgent transport should be made within the first hours; analgesia with a nerve block, pressure care, hydration and delirium prevention continue while waiting.

generation.uncertainty_note: The 2016 edition of the Standard specified 48 hours; the 2023 revision reduced the timeframe to 36 hours in line with the ANZ Hip Fracture Registry benchmark. Reviewers should confirm the current wording of quality statement 5 before publication, as many local pathways still quote 48 hours.

references.title: Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard (2023)
references.locator: Quality statement 5 - Timing of surgery

references.title: Australian and New Zealand Hip Fracture Registry - Annual Report
references.locator: Key performance indicators - time to surgery

tutor_context: Key facts: the Standard also expects pain assessment within 30 minutes of arrival with analgesia including nerve blocks, orthogeriatric care, mobilisation the day after surgery, and secondary fracture prevention; for rural patients the time to surgery includes transfer, so early referral matters; delirium prevention and pressure care start in the referring hospital. Common misconceptions: that the clock starts on arrival at the operating hospital; that 48 hours remains the benchmark. Out of scope: choice of arthroplasty versus fixation.
plan: Tests recall of the national time-to-surgery benchmark for hip fracture, which drives transfer urgency from a rural site (outcomes 1.7, 1.4). An older woman with a neck of femur fracture presents to a hospital that cannot operate and transport is offered in 3 days. Distractors are the older 48-hour figure and other plausible intervals. Supported by the ACSQHC Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are working in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital at 19:00; a registrar is on site overnight. A 55-year-old man fell from his bicycle at low speed 90 minutes ago, striking his helmeted head on the road. Bystanders report he was unresponsive for less than a minute. He cannot remember the 5 minutes before the fall. He has vomited once in the department, has a mild frontal headache and has a small scalp haematoma over the right parietal region with no palpable step and no laceration. There are no signs of a basal skull fracture, his pupils are equal and reactive and there is no focal neurological deficit. His GCS has been 15 since the ambulance arrived. He takes no antiplatelet or anticoagulant medication and has not been drinking alcohol. The registrar asks you to apply the head injury guideline's CT criteria.
lead_in: Which single finding, if present, would make a CT brain mandatory for this patient?

options.text: A single episode of vomiting
Amnesia for the 5 minutes before impact
Two or more episodes of vomiting
A scalp haematoma without a palpable skull defect

explanations.A: A single vomit after a head injury is common and is not by itself a CT criterion in the Canadian CT Head Rule used in Australian guidelines; it does warrant a period of observation.
explanations.B: Retrograde amnesia becomes a criterion only when it exceeds 30 minutes before impact; 5 minutes does not meet the threshold.
explanations.C: Two or more episodes of vomiting is a high-risk criterion, alongside a GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture and age 65 or over. Any one of these mandates CT. He currently has none, so structured neurological observations and reassessment of his GCS at 2 hours are the plan, with a CT if he vomits again or his GCS drops.
explanations.D: A scalp haematoma on its own is not a criterion; it becomes relevant only if there is a palpable depression, a large boggy haematoma suggesting fracture, or signs of basal skull fracture.

learning_point: In a GCS 15 adult with minor head injury, two or more episodes of vomiting is one of the high-risk features (with GCS below 15 at 2 hours, suspected skull fracture, age 65 or over and anticoagulation) that mandates CT; a single vomit, a small scalp haematoma or brief amnesia alone do not.
setting_note: In a rural hospital without CT, a patient who meets a CT criterion needs transfer for imaging, while one who does not can be observed locally with structured neurological observations and discharged with written head injury advice to a responsible adult.

generation.uncertainty_note: The item uses the Canadian CT Head Rule criteria as adopted in Australian adult head injury guidelines; local SA Health pathways may add criteria such as anticoagulant use or lower the threshold for imaging.

references.title: NSW Institute of Trauma and Injury Management - Initial Management of Closed Head Injury in Adults (2nd edition), incorporating the Canadian CT Head Rule
references.locator: Risk assessment and indications for CT in mild head injury

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology
references.locator: Head injury - assessment and indications for imaging

tutor_context: Key facts: Canadian CT Head Rule high-risk criteria are GCS below 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture, two or more vomits, and age 65 or over; medium-risk criteria are retrograde amnesia over 30 minutes and a dangerous mechanism; anticoagulant use is a separate indication in Australian practice; discharge requires a responsible adult and written advice. Common misconceptions: that any loss of consciousness mandates CT; that a scalp haematoma means a skull fracture. Out of scope: paediatric head injury rules.
plan: Tests recall of the CT criteria for minor head injury in an adult with GCS 15 (outcomes 1.4, 1.5). A middle-aged cyclist has brief loss of consciousness, one vomit, short amnesia and a scalp haematoma, none of which mandates CT. Distractors are the near-miss versions of real criteria. Supported by the NSW ITIM adult head injury guideline and the Canadian CT Head Rule.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident covering the emergency department and ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre overnight. A 79-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter at 23:00. Three hours earlier, after an argument, she swallowed 20 tablets of immediate-release paracetamol 500 mg (10 g) from a packet of 24. She weighs 62 kg, took nothing else and does not drink alcohol. She is alert and orientated with normal observations and feels mildly nauseated. Her only regular medicine is perindopril. The hospital laboratory can run a paracetamol concentration with a turnaround of about one hour, and the Poisons Information Centre is available on 13 11 26. She says she regrets what she did and asks to go home.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing the paracetamol ingestion?

options.text: Measure the serum paracetamol concentration at 4 hours after ingestion and treat according to the nomogram
Give activated charcoal 50 g orally now
Start intravenous acetylcysteine immediately without waiting for a concentration
Observe overnight and check liver function tests at 24 hours

explanations.A: For a single acute immediate-release ingestion presenting within 8 hours, the decision to treat rests on a paracetamol concentration taken 4 hours or more after ingestion and plotted on the Australian and New Zealand nomogram, with acetylcysteine started if the level is on or above the treatment line. Her level can be drawn in an hour and reported before 8 hours have elapsed, so this is the correct pathway. The Poisons Information Centre should be called, and she must not be discharged before the result and a mental health risk assessment.
explanations.B: Activated charcoal is recommended within 2 hours of an immediate-release overdose of 10 g or more, and up to 4 hours only for massive or modified-release ingestions. At 3 hours after 10 g it is not indicated.
explanations.C: Empirical acetylcysteine is started when the concentration cannot be obtained and acted on within 8 hours of ingestion, or for massive, staggered or late presentations. Here the level will be available well inside 8 hours, so treatment is guided by the nomogram; starting acetylcysteine would not be dangerous, but it is not the best next step.
explanations.D: Liver function tests are normal in the first 24 hours even after serious overdose; waiting for them misses the window in which acetylcysteine is most effective.

learning_point: For a single acute immediate-release paracetamol overdose presenting within 8 hours, the decision to start acetylcysteine is based on a paracetamol concentration taken at least 4 hours after ingestion plotted on the nomogram; acetylcysteine is started empirically only if the level cannot be obtained before 8 hours.
setting_note: In a country hospital whose laboratory cannot return a paracetamol concentration within 8 hours of ingestion, start acetylcysteine empirically and stop it if the level is later below the line; discuss every overdose with the Poisons Information Centre and arrange a mental health assessment, which may be by telehealth.

references.title: Guidelines for the management of paracetamol poisoning in Australia and New Zealand (Chiew AL et al., Medical Journal of Australia, 2020 update)
references.locator: Acute immediate-release ingestion presenting within 8 hours - timing of paracetamol concentration, nomogram and activated charcoal

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology
references.locator: Paracetamol poisoning - assessment and acetylcysteine

tutor_context: Key facts: toxic dose threshold is 10 g or 200 mg/kg; the nomogram line starts at 150 mg/L at 4 hours; charcoal is for presentation within 2 hours (4 hours for massive or modified-release); empirical acetylcysteine if the level will not be available within 8 hours; older patients and those on enzyme-inducing drugs are not treated differently under the current guideline; every deliberate overdose requires a mental health risk assessment and safe-keeping of medicines. Common misconceptions: that normal early liver function tests are reassuring; that a remorseful patient can go home. Out of scope: the two-bag acetylcysteine regimen and massive ingestion thresholds.
plan: Tests the standard assessment pathway for an acute paracetamol overdose presenting at 3 hours (outcomes 1.7, 1.9, 1.4). An older woman at a country hospital with an on-site laboratory asks to go home. Distractors are charcoal outside its window, empirical acetylcysteine when a timely level is available, and watchful waiting. Supported by the Australian and New Zealand paracetamol poisoning guideline.

stem: You are the only doctor on site overnight in the 4-bed emergency department of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula; the GP is on call from home. At 02:10 a 58-year-old man is brought in by his wife. They were watching television together when, at 01:30, he suddenly stopped speaking properly and his right arm went weak. On examination he has expressive dysphasia, right facial droop and right arm power 2 out of 5; he is alert. Blood pressure is 172/94 mmHg, heart rate 88 and regular, SpO2 97% on room air and bedside glucose 6.2 mmol/L. He has hypertension and takes no anticoagulant, has had no recent surgery or bleeding, and his wife asks whether you can give him an aspirin.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give aspirin 300 mg orally now and reassess his deficit in one hour
Activate the acute stroke pathway now and call for time-critical imaging and reperfusion assessment
Phone the GP on call and ask them to come in and assess him before any further decisions are made
Admit him for observation and arrange a CT brain and physician review in the morning

explanations.A: Aspirin is withheld until intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded on imaging, and it is not given before thrombolysis. Reassessing in an hour wastes time within the treatment window.
explanations.B: A sudden focal deficit with a witnessed onset 40 minutes ago is a time-critical emergency: he may be eligible for thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and thrombectomy beyond that. The junior doctor's job is to activate the stroke pathway immediately, which in this setting means phoning the state stroke or telestroke service and the retrieval service for urgent transfer to a CT-capable, thrombolysis-capable hospital, while recording the onset time, checking glucose and keeping him nil by mouth. In a hospital with CT it means calling the stroke code and going straight to the scanner.
explanations.C: The GP on call should be informed, but waiting for them to arrive before activating the pathway delays reperfusion; both calls can be made in parallel and the stroke call comes first.
explanations.D: Overnight observation treats a hyperacute stroke as a routine admission and removes any chance of reperfusion therapy.

learning_point: A sudden focal neurological deficit with a known onset time is a time-critical emergency: activate the stroke pathway immediately and arrange urgent imaging and reperfusion assessment, and do not give aspirin until haemorrhage has been excluded on CT.
setting_note: In a tertiary hospital this means calling the stroke code and going straight to CT; in a rural hospital without CT it means an immediate call to the retrieval service and the state telestroke or on-call stroke service, with the GP on call informed in parallel rather than waited for.

references.title: Stroke Foundation - Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
references.locator: Pre-hospital and emergency assessment; reperfusion therapy eligibility and time windows; antiplatelet therapy after imaging

references.title: SA Health Statewide Stroke Clinical Network - acute stroke and telestroke pathways for rural sites
references.locator: Rural acute stroke pathway - early notification and retrieval

tutor_context: Key facts: thrombolysis is considered up to 4.5 hours from onset and thrombectomy up to 24 hours in selected patients, so every minute counts; glucose must be checked to exclude hypoglycaemia as a mimic; aspirin is given only after haemorrhage is excluded and not within 24 hours of thrombolysis; record the time last known well, medications and contraindications for the receiving team. Common misconceptions: that aspirin is harmless to give early; that the stroke call should wait for a senior doctor to confirm the diagnosis. Out of scope: thrombolysis dosing and blood pressure thresholds.
plan: Tests immediate activation of the stroke pathway by a junior doctor (outcomes 1.9, 1.7) in a way that applies to any setting. A man with a witnessed onset of dysphasia and hemiparesis 40 minutes earlier presents overnight and his wife asks for aspirin. Distractors are early aspirin, waiting for the GP on call, and overnight observation. Supported by the Stroke Foundation guidelines.

stem: You are the intern covering the emergency department and ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre overnight; the GP is on call from home. A 78-year-old man presents at 03:00 with 45 minutes of central chest heaviness radiating to the left arm, with nausea and sweating. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Observations: heart rate 54 and regular, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96% on room air. The nurse hands you the 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm at 54 per minute, 2 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF, 1 to 2 mm ST depression in leads I and aVL, and no ST change in the anterior leads. An ECG from an admission 2 years ago was normal.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this ECG?

options.text: Acute pericarditis, because of ST elevation in several leads
Early repolarisation, a normal variant that explains the ST elevation
Posterior myocardial infarction, indicated by the ST depression
Inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction requiring immediate reperfusion

explanations.A: Pericarditis produces widespread concave ST elevation, often with PR depression, and does not cause reciprocal ST depression in the lateral leads. Reciprocal change points firmly to infarction.
explanations.B: Early repolarisation is seen in young, healthy people, mainly in the anterior leads, with notched J points and no symptoms. New ST elevation compared with a previously normal ECG in a 78-year-old with typical pain is not a normal variant.
explanations.C: Posterior infarction shows ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves. Here the depression in I and aVL is the reciprocal mirror of the inferior elevation, not a separate territory.
explanations.D: ST elevation of 1 mm or more in two contiguous inferior leads with reciprocal depression in I and aVL is an inferior STEMI. The bradycardia and low-normal blood pressure suggest right ventricular involvement or vagal tone, so nitrates should be used with caution. The intern should give aspirin 300 mg, phone the GP on call and the cardiology or retrieval service immediately, and work through the fibrinolysis checklist, because primary PCI cannot be reached within the recommended time from this hospital.

learning_point: ST elevation in two contiguous leads with reciprocal ST depression in the opposite leads is a STEMI; in a rural hospital far from a catheterisation laboratory this triggers the chest pain pathway for an immediate fibrinolysis decision and transfer.
setting_note: In a tertiary hospital the patient goes straight to the catheterisation laboratory; 90 minutes from a PCI centre, fibrinolysis in the emergency department is usually indicated, so the intern should phone the cardiology on-call or retrieval service and the GP on call at once while giving aspirin and preparing the fibrinolysis checklist.

references.title: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand - Australian Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes
references.locator: Diagnosis of ST-elevation myocardial infarction; reperfusion strategy where primary PCI is not available within the recommended time

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Acute coronary syndromes - STEMI recognition and reperfusion

tutor_context: Key facts: STEMI criteria are new ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads (1 mm in most leads, higher thresholds in V2 to V3 depending on age and sex); reciprocal depression increases specificity; inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension suggests right ventricular involvement, in which nitrates can cause profound hypotension and right-sided leads (V4R) help; fibrinolysis is indicated when primary PCI cannot be achieved within about 90 to 120 minutes of first medical contact. Common misconceptions: that ST elevation in more than one lead group means pericarditis; that a slow heart rate is reassuring. Out of scope: fibrinolytic drug selection and contraindication lists.
plan: Tests ECG interpretation of an inferior STEMI with reciprocal changes by a solo rural intern (outcomes 1.5, 1.9). An older diabetic man with typical pain has inferior ST elevation, lateral ST depression and bradycardia. Distractors are pericarditis, early repolarisation and posterior infarction, each anchored on one feature. Supported by the NHF/CSANZ acute coronary syndrome guidelines.
